newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran MPs swing behind moderate president-elect.
newsitem.headline: Iran MPs swing behind moderate president-elect.

text.p: Iran's conservative Islamic clergy-dominated parliament swung behind the country's moderate president-elect on Sunday in a dramatic political about-face after his huge election victory.
The Islamic republic's outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani also offered to help his successor Mohammad Khatami carry out his programmes and plans.
The handover is due to take place in August.

More than 200 members of the 270-seat Majlis sent a message to Khatami pledging to cooperate fully. The assembly reopened on Sunday after a two-week recess for what turned out to be Iran's fiercest election campaign since the 1979 revolution led by the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

"No doubt this great epic is a reinforcement of the ideals of the late Imam Khomeini and a renewal of allegiance with the supreme leader of the Islamic revolution, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei," deputies said in a statement read in open session.
Nearly 200 deputies had supported Khatami's conservative rival, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, in the campaign for Friday's election and only 70 backed Khatami.
But Khatami won by a landslide -- 69 percent of a huge turnout of more than 29 million of Iran's 33 million electorate -- and trounced the speaker, who had to settle for 25 percent.

Khatami, in his first comment since the election, said in a statement on Tehran radio he hoped he could prove he deserved such popular support. All groups should participate in making a prosperous, free and independent Iran, he said, stressing the rule of law.
The defeated Nateq-Nouri told the Majlis the massive turnout had surprised Western analysts. Henceforth, the Majlis would be an ally to Khatami and his government, he said.

Rafsanjani, who must step down after serving the maximum two consecutive four-year terms permitted by law, will continue to exercise powerful influence as head of a council of advisers which mediates any dispute between parliament and another body of clerics and lawyers.
At a two-hour news conference Rafsanjani said his government's success in reconstructing the country and reducing dependence on foreigners had been his sweetest achievement.
The bitterest points included "not having the desired programme with littoral states of the Persian Gulf or a solution in Palestine".
Rafsanjani said he did not think his reconstruction programme would be slowed under Khatami's presidency but rather would be expedited.
He said the election had shown that the Iranian people were more politicised and aware. The growth of understanding among people spoke of good news of social development.
In editorials assessing the surprise outcome of the polls Iranian newspapers said the people had sent a message which must not go unheeded.

"There was once a time when it was popularly believed that the sky would fall on the day the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, the late Imam Khomeini, ceased to live," said the English daily Iran News.
But he had died and one of his closest disciples, Khamenei, had filled the gap. It said the election confirmed that a philosophy, not a person, was the basis of the Islamic system.
Tehran Times said with the majority in the Majlis belonging to Nateq-Nouri's camp the new president may face some problems with the legislature.
